questions.question: Explain the process of catagenesis and its important in hydrocarbon generation. [U] / [CO1]
questions.solution_html:
• • Catagenesis is the intermediate stage in the transformation of buried organic matter, where
  • increasing heat and pressure (about 60–120°C) break down kerogen through thermal cracking.
  • This temperature range is called the oil window , where kerogen decomposes into liquid
  • hydrocarbons (oil) and gaseous hydrocarbons (natural gas). (1.5 marks)
  • • It is highly significant because different types of kerogen generate varying amounts of oil
  • and gas, and the efficiency of catagenesis determines how much hydrocarbon a source rock
  • can produce. The process also influences the physical and chemical properti es of the
  • hydrocarbons, affecting their migration and accumulation in reservoir rocks. Thus,
  • catagenesis is a key stage directly linked to economic hydrocarbon generation. (1.5 marks)

questions.question: Summarize the implications of nitrogen compounds for crude oil pricing? [U] [4]
questions.solution_html:
• • The presence of nitrogen compounds in crude oil can significantly impact pricing due to
  • their influence on refining efficiency and product yield.
  • • High nitrogen content is often associated with heavier, lower -quality crudes, which may
  • require more extensive and costly processing.
  • • Lighter crudes with minimal nitrogen content are favored for their easier processing and
  • higher yields of valuable products.

questions.question: Explain the significance of understanding the composition of oxygen compounds in crude oil.
questions.solution_html:
• [U] / [CO4]
  • Understanding the composition of oxygen compounds in crude oil is important because these
  • components—such as alcohols, phenols, and ketones —affect key properties like viscosity,
  • volatility, and overall crude quality. Excessive oxygen content can make crude oil unstable by
  • promoting oxidation, leading to the formation of acids, gums, and deposits that corrode equipment
  • and clog pipelines. Knowing the types and amounts of oxygen compounds helps refineries
  • manage storage conditions, use appropriate additives, and prevent degradation, ensuring efficient
  • processing and safe handling of crude oil. (Any 3 Points – Give full credit)

questions.question: Explain the significance of a high calorific value for a fuel [U] [5]
questions.solution_html:
• • Calorific value is the amount of energy released when a unit mass or volume of fuel is
  • completely burned, typically expressed in mega joules per kilogram (MJ/kg) or mega joules
  • per cubic meter (MJ/m³).
  • • It is a critical measure for evaluating the energy content of fuels, influencing their efficiency
  • and suitability for various applications.
  • • Higher calorific values indicate more energy -efficient fuels, making them preferable for
  • combustion processes in power generation, transportation, and heating.

questions.question: Explain how does pour point impact the usability of fuels? [U] / [CO5]
questions.solution_html:
• The pour point is the lowest temperature at which a fuel remains fluid and can flow. It directly
  • impacts fuel usability, especially in cold climates. Fuels with a high pour point may thicken or
  • solidify at low temperatures, causing flow problems in pipelines, storage tanks, and engines. This
  • can lead to reduced efficiency, ignition issues, and equipment damage. Therefore, understanding
  • and controlling the pour point is essential to ensure smooth handling, transport, and performance
  • of fuels under varying temperature cond itions. (Pour point definition 1 mark, explanation 2
  • marks)

questions.question: What is primary migration in the context of petroleum formation, and how does it differ from secondary
questions.solution_html:
• migration?
  • (Explanation on primary migration 3.5 marks, secondary migration 3.5 marks)
  • • 1° migration: Migration of petroleum starts in the source rocks. Primary migration refers to
  • the initial movement of hydrocarbons from the source rock, where they are generated, to the
  • adjacent carrier beds. Primary migration is closely tied to the generation of hydrocarbons.
  • • 2° migration : The movement of petroleum from the source rock to the reservoir rock is
  • called 2° migration , often facilitated by geological structures like faults and fractures. This
  • focuses on the accumulation and trapping of these hydrocarbons in suitable reservoir rocks.
  • During migration composition of petroleum may differ due to filtration, adsorption, and reaction
  • with elements like sulphur. The cap rocks of the basement rock should have low permeability
  • than the reservoir rock to prevent the escape of oil and gas.

questions.question: Explain the differences be tween proved , probable , and possible reserves in petroleum
questions.solution_html:
• exploration. [U] / [CO2]
  • (Any 2 points each for proved, probable, and possible reserves Give Full credit)
  • Proved, probable, and possible reserves represent different levels of confidence in the
  • recoverability of petroleum resources and are essential for evaluating the economic potential of
  • an oil or gas field. Proved reserves are the most reliable estimates. They refer to quantities of
  • petroleum that can be recovered with reasonable certainty from known reservoirs under current
  • economic conditions, operating methods, and government regulations. In deterministic methods,
  • this means a high degree of confidence, while in probabilistic terms, there is at least a 90%
  • probability of recovery. Proved reserves are further subdivided into developed (ready for
  • production) and undeveloped (requiring additional drilling or infrastructure).
  • Probable reserves fall under unproved reserves but have a higher likelihood of being recovered
  • compared to possible reserves. They rely on geological and engineering data but lack the certainty
  • of proved reserves due to technical or economic uncertainties. Probable reserve s are considered
  • more likely than not to be recoverable, typically with at least a 50% probability. However, they
  • may not be extracted if economic conditions make recovery unfeasible.
  • Possible reserves represent the least certain category among the three. They are also unproved
  • reserves but have a lower chance of successful extraction compared to probable reserves.
  • Geological and engineering data indicate that they are less likely to be recovered , with a
  • probability of at least 10%. These reserves often depend on future technological improvements
  • or changes in economic conditions to become viable.
  • The key difference lies in the degree of confidence: proved reserves offer the highest certainty of
  • commercial recovery, probable reserves indicate moderate confidence, and possible reserves
  • reflect low confidence, making them the most uncertain category in petroleum exploration.

questions.question: Explain the significance of metallic and organo metallic hydrocarbons in crude oil and their
questions.solution_html:
• implications for refining.
  • (Any three points on s ignificance of m etallic constituent 3.5 marks, o rgano metallic
  • hydrocarbon 3.5 marks)
  • • Metallic constituents, such as nickel, vanadium, and iron, are often found in crude oil and
  • can have profound effects on refining efficiency and product quality. The presence of these
  • metals can also cause fouling in equipment, resulting in increased maintenance costs and
  • operational downtime, cause corrosion of refinery equipment.
  • • Organometallic hydrocarbons, which contain metal atoms bonded to organic molecules, can
  • be significant in crude oil and its refining processes. The presence of organometallic
  • compounds can complicate the behavior of catalysts and may lead to unwanted side
  • reactions, resulting in decreased efficiency and product yield.

questions.question: Explain the impact of olefins on the refining process of crude oil. [U] / [CO4]
questions.solution_html:
• (Any 5 points give 7 marks)
  • Olefins are unsaturated hydrocarbons, which means the double bond is present between the two
  • carbon atoms in the formula. The generic formula is (CnH2n), and the lowest member of this
  • homologous series is ethylene, C 2H4.This series is known as alkenes. These are highly reactive
  • and can react to themselves to mono olefins. Olefins are not present in crude oil, but they are
  • produced by thermal and catalytic decomposition or dehydrogenation of normal paraffins. Olefins
  • can complicate the refining process because their double bonds make them more reactive, which
  • can lead to polymerization or other unwanted reactions. They are often targeted for conversion
  • into more stable compounds during refining. Olefins are generally undesirable in finished products
  • because, the double bonds are reactive and the compounds are more easily oxidized and
  • polymerized to form gums and varnishes, so they can be removed by absorption in sulfuric
  • acid.The reactivity of olefins makes them valuable feedstocks in the petrochemical industry,
  • particularly in the production of polymers, synthetic fibers, and chemicals.

questions.solution_html:
• quality.[U][5] (Give full credit to 7 points)
  • • The refractive index of a hydrocarbon is a measure of how much light bends as it passes
  • through the substance.
  • • It is defined as the ratio of the speed of light in a vacuum to the speed of light in the
  • medium.
  • • It provides valuable information about their composition, purity, and concentration.
  • • A higher refractive index often correlates with a higher conce ntration of aromatic
  • compounds
  • • A higher refractive index can impact the performance and characteristics of the final
  • product.
  • • Refractive index measurements can assist in identifying different types of hydrocarbons,
  • such as alkanes, alkenes, and aromatics.
  • • By monitoring the refractive index, manufacturers can ensure compliance with industry
  • standards and maintain product consistency, ultimately enhancing operational efficiency
  • and safety.
